newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia sees brighter 1998 on low yields, deficit.
newsitem.headline: Russia sees brighter 1998 on low yields, deficit.

text.p: Russian ministers, forecasting economic success next year, said on Thursday the economy would return to growth and companies would win cheaper finance to fund much-needed investment.
"We are now at the point of breakthrough," First Deputy Economy Minister Ivan Materov told a news briefing after a cabinet meeting on the 1998 budget and the medium-term outlook.

Echoing upbeat predictions from several senior ministers, he said Russian gross domestic product would rise about two percent in 1998. Ministers once forecast two percent growth this year, but they now expect flat output or a slim two percent fall.

First Deputy Finance Minister Vladimir Petrov told the same briefing that yields on government securities markets would fall to 12-14 percent in 1998, while the central bank refinancing rate would fall to 20 percent. He expected inflation of five percent.

"This will naturally allow credit to become accessible -- it's already becoming accessible," Petrov said, adding that farmers had borrowed money commercially this year to complete their sowing campaign.
"Accessibility is becoming a reality, and in 1998 this reality has got to be strengthened."
Russian entrepreneurs say high real interest rates, along with a heavy and arbitrary tax burden, are strangling production and stifling the economy as a whole.
Government figures presented to the State Duma, the lower house of parliament, this week forecast a five percent drop in investment this year, after a steep 18 percent fall last year.
Yields on discount Russian Treasury bills are now around 20 percent, the level the Finance Ministry forecast for the end of the year, while the refinancing rate is 36 percent.

Petrov said lower yields on government securities would also help to push down the budget deficit to 4.6 percent of gross domestic product in 1998 and to 3.5 percent of GDP by 2000, raising the possibility of less foreign borrowing.

Russia said on Thursday it would place $3 billion in 1998, but Petrov said Eurobonds would slip in importance. "We will continue to work with Eurobonds, but their attractiveness compared to internal securities is lessening," he said.
The total budget deficit in 1997 by international standards is about seven percent.
Reducing the budget deficit in 1998 also depends on better tax collection after officials raked in just 65 percent of target levels so far this year.
Failure to meet revenue targets has forced the government to submit plans to cut 1997 spending by a fifth to parliament, which is due to consider the plans next week.
The government also wants deputies to approve a new tax code before it starts its summer break and it says the 1998 budget, to be presented to parliament at the end of August, will be based on that.
The battle will not be easy.
The State Duma, dominated by communists, opposes government plans to cut spending across the board and to slash costly rent and housing subsidies.
Deputies are also angry at Russia's privatisation efforts, accusing ministers of selling property off too cheaply.
On Thursday they approved a draft bill which says the cabinet broke the law privatising state assets worth billions of dollars in what was dubbed the biggest sell-off in history.
The bill, which is not binding on the government, says privatisation in 1992-1996 was unsatisfactory and it calls on the cabinet to correct its mistakes.
The chamber is expected to pass the draft finally next week after considering ammendments.
Russian officials expect to raise 10-15 trillion roubles ($2.6 billion) for the budget from privatisation this year.
--Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520 ($ = 5766 Russian Roubles)
